name: Apocalyptic Literature: Hope in Persecution

objectives.text: Identify Revelation as the last book of the Bible, which tells that Jesus is coming again and that God will make all things new
Name John as the follower of Jesus who wrote down the vision while he was sent away to the island of Patmos for telling about Jesus
Retell the promise that God will wipe away every tear and end death, crying, and pain in the new heaven and new earth
State that Revelation shows Jesus as the King of kings who defeats evil and wins in the end
Recite one of the songs of praise sung around God's throne in Revelation and identify who is being praised
Describe how John saw the risen Jesus in glory in his first vision and what Jesus told him not to fear
Explain that Revelation uses picture language such as dragons, beasts, and a Lamb to show real truths about God, Christ, and evil
Explain that apocalypse means an unveiling and that Revelation uncovers the heavenly reality behind earthly events
Compare the Lion of Judah and the slain Lamb in John's vision to explain how Christ conquers through his death
Identify an encouragement, a warning, and a promise that Jesus gives to one of the seven churches
Identify the features of apocalyptic writing, including visions, angelic guides, symbolic numbers and creatures, cosmic conflict, and God's final triumph, in Daniel and Revelation
Explain how the first readers' situation of persecution and pressure to worship the emperor shapes Revelation's message of hope and endurance
Analyze the symbolic meaning of numbers such as 7, 12, and 666 in Revelation by tracing how these numbers are used elsewhere in Scripture
Connect images in Revelation to their Old Testament sources in Daniel, Ezekiel, and Zechariah to show how Scripture interprets Scripture
Analyze Jesus' teaching in the Olivet Discourse as apocalyptic instruction that calls disciples to watchfulness and endurance rather than speculation
Explain the Reformed confession of Christ's visible return and the last judgment and relate it to John's vision of the great white throne
Compare the garden of Genesis with the new Jerusalem of Revelation to show how the Bible's story ends in restored creation and God dwelling with his people
Explain the preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist approaches to reading Revelation and the strengths and weaknesses of each
Compare the amillennial, postmillennial, and premillennial readings of the thousand years, noting which views have been common in the Reformed tradition
Analyze the structure of Revelation, including how the cycles of seals, trumpets, and bowls may retell the same period with increasing intensity
Construct a study of the throne room vision that explains how heavenly worship reframes the suffering of the church on earth
Evaluate the practice of setting dates for Christ's return in light of Jesus' teaching that no one knows the day or hour
Defend from Revelation the Reformed doctrine that God governs all of history, including the actions of persecutors, for his purposes
Evaluate how Revelation's call to faithful witness and patient endurance applies to Christians facing persecution today
Create a presentation tracing the theme of the Lamb from the Passover and the prophets to the worship of the Lamb as the climax of Revelation

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (identifying Revelation, John on Patmos, Jesus' victory, wiping away tears, meaning of apocalypse, Lion and Lamb, numbers, purpose for suffering Christians, Old Testament connections, four interpretive approaches, throne room study, date-setting, God's sovereignty, worship of the Lamb). Dropped 'observe strange creatures' and 'heaven as a place with no more pain' as filler or duplicates and folded them into objectives on picture language and the new creation. Added the risen Christ vision, the songs of praise, the letters to the seven churches, apocalyptic genre features, historical setting, the Olivet Discourse, the last judgment, Genesis and Revelation compared, millennial views, Revelation's structure, and application to persecution today. Supplied verse-level Scripture and confessional anchors (WCF 1.9, 5.1, 33; WSC Q11, Q26, Q38; HC Q52, Q58; Belgic 37) where they state the doctrine taught.
